findings.claim: For this part of the course you study two contemporary music videos in depth, alongside a video from the 1980s or 1990s. One pairing is Lizzo’s Good as Hell or Taylor Swift’s The Man. The second pairing — the focus of this lesson — is Stormzy’s Superheroes (2020) or Justin Bieber’s Intentions (2020).
findings.problem: Misdescribes the structure of the music section. The specification sets option pairs in which a class studies ONE contemporary music video (and its online media) together with ONE 1980s/1990s music video — not two contemporary videos plus an older one, and not one video chosen from each of two 'contemporary pairings'. The supplied guidance states plainly that the class studies one contemporary option pair set by their teacher.
findings.correction: For this part of the course your class studies one option pair set by your teacher: one contemporary music video and its online media, together with one music video from the 1980s or 1990s. The contemporary options include Lizzo's Good as Hell, Taylor Swift's The Man, Stormzy's Superheroes (2020) and Justin Bieber's Intentions (2020). This lesson focuses on Superheroes, with notes on Intentions.

findings.claim: remember that you must also know the artist’s official website and at least two social or participatory media platforms connected to it
findings.correction: remember that you must also know the artist's official website and the social and participatory media connected to it
findings.problem: Invented requirement: neither the fact sheet nor the quoted assessment rules specify a minimum number of social or participatory media platforms to be studied. 'At least two' is an unsupported exam requirement.

findings.claim: they recognised that the song samples Keisha White’s Someday
findings.problem: The fact sheet says Stormzy 'use[s] ... lyrics from Keisha White's Someday, which feature at the end of the Superheroes track' — an interpolation of the lyrics, not a sample of her recording.
findings.correction: they recognised Stormzy's use of lyrics from Keisha White's Someday at the end of the track

findings.claim: His #Merky brand donated £500,000 to the Black Heart Foundation for scholarships and pledged £10 million over ten years to fight racial inequality in the UK.
findings.problem: The fact sheet attributes the £500,000 donation to the Black Heart Foundation to Stormzy himself (in 2020), and separately attributes the £10m over ten years pledge to his #Merky brand.
findings.correction: In 2020 Stormzy donated £500,000 to the Black Heart Foundation for scholarships, and his #Merky brand has pledged £10 million over ten years to fight racial inequality in the UK.

findings.claim: In the exam, you will not be given a copy of The Sun to analyse.
findings.problem: This contradicts the specification's assessment rules. For Component 1 Section A the spec states that 'Copies of the relevant set products will be provided by WJEC Eduqas in the examination' and that learners 'refer to copies of the set products in the examination in both questions one and two', and newspapers are one of the print forms that may be assessed in Section A. The claim is only true of Section B, where no copies are supplied, and as written it misleads students about exam procedure.
findings.correction: In Section B, questions on The Sun test what you know about it as an example of a newspaper industry and how it reaches and targets its audience, so you answer from your own knowledge rather than from a copy of the paper. (In Section A, where newspapers may be assessed for media language or representation, a copy of the set product is provided.)

findings.claim: For Section B questions on The Sun, examiners want named facts — figures, dates, named schemes and named bodies — not descriptions of a front page.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about examiner behaviour. The specification's assessment rules say only that Questions 3 and 4 are stepped questions assessing knowledge and understanding of media industries and audiences; they make no claim about what examiners 'want' or reward.
findings.correction: Section B questions assess knowledge and understanding of media industries and audiences, so support each point with specific detail about The Sun — a figure, a named scheme, a named platform or the named regulator — rather than a general statement about newspapers or a description of a front page.

findings.claim: launching gambling brands such as Sun Bingo, Sun Vegas and Sun Bets
findings.problem: Unsupported by the fact sheets: both set-product factsheets name only 'Sun Vegas' and 'Sun Bets' as examples of The Sun's diversification. 'Sun Bingo' is not mentioned in the board's material (it also appears in the Key Fact box and the conclusion).
findings.correction: launching gambling brands such as Sun Vegas and Sun Bets

findings.claim: {"q": "What gambling brand did The Sun launch as part of its diversification strategy?", "a": "Sun Bingo."}
findings.problem: The board's factsheets name Sun Vegas and Sun Bets as The Sun's gambling diversification brands; Sun Bingo is unsupported by the sheet, so the answer should use a sheet-supported example.
findings.correction: {"q": "Name one gambling brand The Sun launched as part of its diversification strategy.", "a": "Sun Vegas (or Sun Bets)."}

findings.claim: no copy is given in the exam, so you must know the specific details from memory
findings.problem: The assessment rules only state that copies of set products are provided for Component 1 Section A (questions 1 and 2); they make no statement at all about whether material is or is not supplied for the Section B industries/audiences questions. Asserting that no copy is given is an exam-procedure claim the specification does not make (unsupported by the quoted rules).
findings.correction: Questions on this set product test media industry and audience knowledge directly, so learn the specific facts and figures thoroughly. When a question asks you to explain funding, ownership or regulation, name the BBC, the licence fee and Ofcom explicitly and explain how each applies to Desert Island Discs.

findings.claim: The most common mistake is writing generally about video games instead of using Fortnite’s own facts
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about candidate behaviour/frequency of errors. Neither the quoted specification (version 10) nor the set product fact sheet makes any claim about the most common mistake candidates make on this question.
findings.correction: A safer approach is to anchor every point in Fortnite’s own facts rather than writing generally about video games — always name Epic Games, Tencent, specific figures or named streamers rather than writing vaguely about ‘the game industry’.

findings.claim: along with randomly assigned character skins reducing overt racism or misogyny among players
findings.problem: The fact sheet states this tentatively: 'there seems to be little racism or misogyny expressed by the players compared to other videogames - perhaps because free players are randomly assigned race and gender skins'. The lesson presents a speculative explanation as established fact.
findings.correction: along with the suggestion that randomly assigning race and gender ‘skins’ to free players may reduce overt racism or misogyny among players

findings.claim: Compare how gender is represented in the 1956 Quality Street advert and the 2023 NHS 111 advert. Refer to both products in your answer.  [type: 25 marks — Compare with Unseen Resource]
findings.problem: The assessment rules state that Question 2 part (b) (25 marks) 'will require a comparison of an unseen resource with a set product in the same media form'. The task set here compares two set products against each other, which is not the exam task for this tariff and trains the wrong answer structure (the exam always supplies one unseen resource).
findings.correction: Compare how gender is represented in the 1956 Quality Street advert and an unseen print advertisement provided by your teacher. Refer to both the set product and the unseen resource in your answer.

findings.claim: Analyse how the NHS 111 advert represents fatherhood, and draw conclusions about what this suggests about changing gender roles in contemporary Britain.  [type: 20 marks — Analyse and Draw Conclusions]
findings.problem: The assessment rules set only 15-mark (media language), 5-mark (context) and 25-mark (comparison with unseen resource) questions on the Component 1 Section A print products; the 20-mark 'analyse and draw conclusions' tariff belongs to Component 2 (television and music). A 20-mark question on a print advert cannot appear in the exam.
findings.correction: Retype this as a Component 1 task, e.g. 'Analyse how the NHS 111 advert represents fatherhood.' — type: 15 marks — Analyse Media Language (or reframe the representation focus as part of the 25-mark comparison with an unseen resource).

findings.claim: it was an online-only iPlayer channel from 2016 to 2022 (when Man Like Mobeen first aired), before returning to linear broadcast on BBC One
findings.problem: The fact sheet states that BBC Three closed in 2016, existed as an online-only streaming channel, and 'returned to linear television on 1st February 2022... timesharing with CBBC' — i.e. as the BBC Three channel, not on BBC One. It is the programme Man Like Mobeen (series 1) that was later broadcast on BBC One. The lesson conflates the two and gives the wrong broadcaster for BBC Three's return to linear TV.
findings.correction: it was an online-only iPlayer channel from 2016 until BBC Three returned to linear television on 1 February 2022 (timesharing with CBBC), while series 1 of Man Like Mobeen was itself later shown on linear TV on BBC One, and the series is also available on Netflix, allowing audiences to binge-watch it as a boxset.

findings.claim: series 3 peaked at 600,000 viewers and drew more iPlayer requests than the first two series combined
findings.problem: The fact sheet states series 3 'peak[ed] at 600,000 viewers and draw[ing] more iPlayer requests than the first two series' — it does not say 'combined'. The word 'combined' is an unsupported strengthening of the claim.
findings.correction: series 3 peaked at 600,000 viewers and drew more iPlayer requests than the first two series.

findings.claim: it is filmed entirely on location in Small Heath, Birmingham, rather than in a studio
findings.problem: The fact sheet says the programme 'is filmed on location to create a sense of authenticity' and is 'produced on location in Birmingham'; it does not state that every scene is shot on location or that all locations are in Small Heath (the programme is set in Small Heath). 'Entirely' overstates the sheet.
findings.correction: it is filmed on location in Birmingham, in the Small Heath area where it is set, rather than on a studio set
